pieces.title: The door that wasn’t there yesterday
pieces.task: Write the opening of a story in which a character discovers a door that wasn’t there yesterday. End on a cliffhanger.
plan: Who is your character and where are they?
What do they notice first? (use the senses)
How do they feel? Show it, don’t tell it
What happens when they open the door?
criteria: Opens with a hook (action, dialogue or a question)
Varies sentence length; one very short sentence for impact
pieces.starter: The door was green. That was the first wrong thing about it, because nothing on Willow Street had been green since the council painted everything grey.

rubric.name: Story and reader interest
levels: Hooks the reader and keeps them wanting more

rubric.name: Structure and paragraphs
levels: Clear opening, build-up and ending, with linked paragraphs

rubric.name: Sentences and word choice
levels: Some varied sentences and chosen words
Varied sentences for effect, precise vocabulary, show-not-tell

rubric.name: Accuracy
levels: Accurate, including speech and sentence punctuation

pieces.title: Should homework be banned?
pieces.task: Write a speech for your school council arguing EITHER that homework should be banned OR that it should stay. Persuade your audience.
plan: The other side, and why it is wrong
criteria: States the viewpoint clearly at the start
Ends with a call to action
pieces.starter: Imagine coming home after six hours of lessons, only to open your bag and find… more lessons.

rubric.name: Clear viewpoint and reasons
levels: Clear view backed by several developed reasons

rubric.name: Persuasive techniques
levels: Several used well (rhetorical question, rule of three, facts, direct address)

rubric.name: Structure and cohesion
levels: Introduction, ordered paragraphs, counter-argument and strong conclusion, with cohesive adverbials

pieces.title: How does Dickens present Scrooge?
pieces.task: Read the extract from A Christmas Carol (1843). How does Dickens present Scrooge as an unpleasant character? Write two analytical paragraphs.
plan: Point 1: what Dickens shows about Scrooge
Analysis 1: the effect of specific words
criteria: Each paragraph starts with a clear point
Uses short quotations embedded in sentences
Names at least one technique (simile, list, repetition)
Explains the effect of individual words
pieces.starter: Dickens presents Scrooge as cold and selfish from the very first description.

rubric.name: Point answers the question
levels: A point, loosely linked to the question
A clear point that answers the question directly

rubric.name: Evidence
levels: A quotation, but long or not embedded
Short, precise quotations embedded in sentences

rubric.name: Analysis of effect
levels: Names a technique or says what words mean
Explains the effect of specific words on the reader, naming the technique

rubric.name: Link and accuracy
levels: Links back to the question; accurate and formal

pieces.passage: Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster. The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek, stiffened his gait…

pieces.title: Why did William win the Battle of Hastings?
pieces.task: “William won the Battle of Hastings mainly because of Harold’s bad luck.” How far do you agree? Write 3 to 5 paragraphs.
plan: Factor 1 (Harold’s luck: the timing of Hardrada’s invasion, the march) + evidence
Factor 3 (preparation: cavalry, archers, the papal banner) + evidence
Which factor mattered most, and why?
criteria: Gives a clear judgement in the introduction
Uses precise facts: names, dates, places
Uses causal language (because, this meant that, as a result)
Considers a factor other than luck
pieces.starter: Harold Godwinson was certainly unlucky in 1066, but luck alone does not explain the Norman victory.

rubric.name: Clear judgement
levels: A judgement only at the end
A clear judgement in the introduction, carried through

rubric.name: Specific evidence
levels: Precise, accurate facts (names, dates, events) in every paragraph

rubric.name: Explanation
levels: Explains with causal language (because, this led to, as a result) and weighs factors

rubric.name: Counter-view and conclusion
levels: Considers another factor or view and reaches a reasoned conclusion

pieces.title: Which material keeps tea hottest?
pieces.task: A class wrapped four identical cups of hot water (80°C) in different materials and measured the temperature after 20 minutes. Write a conclusion and an evaluation.
plan: What was the result? Quote the numbers
Why? Use the idea of insulation
Was it a fair test? What was kept the same?
How could the investigation be improved?
criteria: States which material was best and worst, with temperatures
Explains using the idea of insulators trapping heat
Names the variable changed, measured and controlled
Suggests repeating readings and finding a mean
pieces.starter: The results show that wool was the best insulator, because the water in that cup was still 62°C after 20 minutes.

rubric.name: States the result using data
levels: Clear result quoting numbers from the results

rubric.name: Explains with science
levels: Explains using the scientific idea (e.g. particles, insulation, forces)

rubric.name: Evaluates the method
levels: Discusses fair testing, repeats or errors, and how to improve

pieces.title: Is our high street thriving?
pieces.task: A class counted the types of shops on a high street. Write up the enquiry: describe the pattern, explain it, and conclude.
plan: What does the data show? Biggest and smallest groups
Why might the high street look like this?
What would make your conclusion more reliable?
Your answer to the enquiry question
criteria: Gives reasons using ideas like online shopping or footfall
Says how reliable the data are (one day? one street?)
pieces.starter: The survey suggests that the high street is changing rather than simply dying.

rubric.name: Describes the pattern
levels: Pattern described with data (numbers, highest, lowest, trend)

rubric.name: Place detail
levels: Specific detail about the place studied

rubric.name: Conclusion and evaluation
levels: A conclusion that answers the enquiry question and says how reliable the data are

pieces.title: Caught in the storm
pieces.task: Write a story about a journey that goes wrong when a storm arrives. Use description to build tension.
plan: Setting the scene: calm before the storm
First signs that something is wrong
criteria: Uses personification or a metaphor for the storm
Includes a short sentence or fragment for impact
A clear ending that links back to the start
pieces.starter: The sky over the estuary was the soft blue of a forget-me-not, and nobody thought to look behind them.

pieces.title: Does temperature affect dissolving?
pieces.task: A group timed how long a sugar cube took to dissolve in water at different temperatures. Write a conclusion and evaluation.
plan: The explanation (particles move faster when warmer)
Fair test: what was kept the same?
criteria: Identifies the independent, dependent and control variables
pieces.starter: The results show that the hotter the water, the faster the sugar dissolved.
